Obstinate

/OB-stih-nit/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Obstinate means not yielding easily to argument or persuasion; stubborn.

The obstinate goat would not budge from the garden path, whatever the farmer tried.

Worked Example

The debate team had lost three rounds in a row using Lena's opening strategy. Her teammates showed her the judges' scoresheets and proposed a different order of arguments. The coach walked her through exactly where the strategy was leaking points. Lena crossed her arms and announced that the team would open the same way in the final round, too. Win or lose, she was too obstinate to change course.

Lena refuses to change her chosen course of action despite clear evidence and repeated arguments from everyone around her — that refusal to yield is what makes her obstinate.

How Obstinate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

stubborn

stubborn: refusing to change one's mind

inflexible

inflexible: unwilling to bend or adapt

Antonyms

flexible

flexible: willing to adapt

accommodating

accommodating: eager to fit others' wishes

How Strong Is It? — stubborn → obstinate → intractable

stubborn vs. obstinate

stubborn vs. obstinate: Stubborn is the everyday, milder word — a child can be stubborn about bedtime; obstinate suggests a more determined, unreasonable refusal to yield to actual arguments.

intractable vs. obstinate

intractable vs. obstinate: Intractable is stronger than obstinate: an intractable person or problem cannot be managed or steered at all, by anyone.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ob-

Prefix — ob-: against; in the way

Root — stin

Root — stin: to stand (Latin stare)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: adjective-forming ending

Put it together

Put it together: Obstinate comes from Latin obstinare, 'to stand firmly against': ob- (against) plus a form of stare, 'to stand.' An obstinate person is literally one who takes a stand and will not be moved off it. The same standing root runs through stationary (standing still), statue (a standing figure), and steadfast.

Use the root in a new word: steadfast

Use the root in a new word: steadfast: Her steadfast support never wavered through the losing season — steadfast, like obstinate, is built on the idea of standing firmly in place, though it wears the idea as a compliment.
